title: Postoperative bleeding
banner: DRAFT, NOT clinically reviewed. Fictional scenario specification; never imported, published or shown to learners.
learning_objectives: Recognise suspected postoperative haemorrhagic shock from combined physiological and wound/drain changes and escalate immediately.
Take first-line nursing actions (reinforce the dressing, mark the drainage, stay with the patient) and tell the surgeon how much has been lost.
Raise anticoagulant doses with the prescriber when bleeding is suspected.
Support fluids and blood products as ordered, and hand over clearly.
Report evolving platelet/coagulation abnormalities alongside blood loss and perfusion without claiming one clotting test establishes a DIC diagnosis or directs component choice.

gaps: No published clinical scenario may exist until the review phase: this is a specification only.
The branching content, consequences and scoring are the author's reading of the cited sources and have had no clinical review.
No source read gives numeric thresholds for blood loss or urine output in this context; none are written.
Fluids, blood products and reversal of anticoagulation are prescribed; the scenario does not say what to give.
The tranexamic acid label read does not cover surgical bleeding and is not used.

This case is a nursing recognition and escalation exercise, not a major-haemorrhage algorithm. Exact emergency call thresholds, component availability, coagulation correction and return-to-theatre decisions remain local clinician decisions.

A 2025 ISTH updated DIC framework and 2026 follow-up review are checked at abstract level only; this surgical case does not teach formal scoring, DIC therapy, emergency transfusion component selection, massive-haemorrhage protocols or viscoelastic interpretation.

setting: A fictional adult in a fictional intensive care unit six hours after abdominal surgery, receiving an anticoagulant for clot prevention.

steps.info: The dressing over the wound is wetter with blood than at the last check. The patient is pale and cold to touch, and the monitor shows a faster pulse and a lower pressure than before.

options.text: Stay with the patient, assess breathing and circulation, call the unit's urgent clinical response for suspected haemorrhagic shock and alert the surgeon promptly. Ask a colleague to quantify wound/drain blood loss and reinforce or mark the dressing without delaying resuscitation assessment.
options.feedback: Blood loss with reduced blood pressure, tachycardia and cool skin may indicate serious postoperative bleeding and shock. The urgent response and bedside assessment take priority over dressing documentation; communicate the wound, drain and physiological trend as the team arrives.
options.consequence: The surgeon is told early, with measurable information, and the team can respond.

options.text: Remove the dressing to look at the wound and put on a clean one without telling anyone.
options.feedback: The first dressing is normally managed by the surgeon; the nurse reinforces it and reports excessive bleeding rather than hiding it under a clean dressing.
options.consequence: The amount of bleeding is no longer visible to the surgeon and the delay costs time.

options.text: Wait for the surgeon's ward round later in the morning and recheck the dressing then.
options.feedback: Excessive bleeding with changes in the vital signs should prompt medical evaluation at once.
options.consequence: The patient continues to lose blood and becomes more unwell.

steps.info: The surgeon has been told and is coming. The patient is now more anxious, and the next dose of the anticoagulant is due.
steps.prompt: What is the best action now?

options.text: Stay with the deteriorating patient, continue haemodynamic assessment, promptly ask the prescriber to reassess the scheduled anticoagulant before it is given, and coordinate the clinical team's ordered investigations, blood products, fluids or theatre transfer with colleagues.
options.feedback: Suspected postoperative haemorrhage needs urgent clinician review of anticoagulation as well as bleeding control and resuscitation. A due medication is not an instruction to ignore active deterioration; dose omission, reversal, component selection and resuscitation orders follow an authorised pathway.
options.consequence: The prescriber decides about the anticoagulant with full information, and the team is ready for the next step.

options.text: Give the anticoagulant on time because it is on the chart, and tell the surgeon afterwards.
options.feedback: An anticoagulant given to a patient who may be bleeding can worsen the haemorrhage; the prescriber must be asked first.
options.consequence: The patient receives a drug that increases the bleeding risk, and the team has to manage the consequence.

options.text: Leave the room to collect blood products you think will be needed.
options.feedback: Leaving an actively deteriorating patient unobserved to collect blood products is unsafe. Stay with the patient and coordinate the urgent team's authorised blood-product preparation through another staff member.
options.consequence: The patient is unobserved for several minutes while deteriorating.

steps.info: The urgent clinical team has assessed the patient and prescribed fluids and blood products, with a possible return to theatre. Urine output is falling, and repeat platelet and coagulation results are pending.

observations.label: Orders
observations.value: Fluids and blood products prescribed by the clinical team

options.text: Provide ordered resuscitation and blood products under emergency transfusion identification and reaction-monitoring procedures; reassess perfusion, urine output and temperature. Communicate blood loss, coagulation, ionized calcium and potassium trends without assigning a DIC diagnosis, and hand over to theatre.
options.feedback: Blood-product selection, emergency issue procedures, haemostatic treatments and return-to-theatre decisions belong to the responsible team. Rapid nursing reassessment and appropriately authorised transfusion safety checks continue while haemorrhage is treated; platelet, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen and D-dimer trends are context for the team and do not by themselves diagnose DIC. During major haemorrhage and transfusion, electrolyte abnormalities including hypocalcaemia and hyperkalaemia can require prompt clinician-directed treatment. Monitor ordered results and temperature, escalate abnormalities, and use the approved warming and major-haemorrhage pathway. Do not independently choose components or electrolyte replacement.
options.consequence: Emergency treatment and transfusion safety checks proceed under the team's direction while bleeding, perfusion and serial laboratory trends are handed over.

options.text: Start the blood immediately without the unit's emergency blood identification and patient-monitoring safeguards because the patient is deteriorating.
options.feedback: Even during major haemorrhage, transfusion follows the hospital's emergency issue and patient-identification pathway, with appropriate safety and reaction monitoring; staff must use its specified emergency checks rather than inventing an exception.
options.consequence: A patient-identification error could cause a serious reaction.

options.text: Stop recording urine output and observations to save time.
options.feedback: Fluid status and urine output are monitored closely in a patient who is bleeding.
options.consequence: The team loses an important measure of how well the patient is being resuscitated.

learning_points: Falling pressure, a fast pulse and cool skin with postoperative wound bleeding justify immediate patient-first assessment and urgent response; measuring and marking wound drainage must not delay getting clinical help.
Do not take the first dressing off and hide the evidence; the surgeon needs to see it.
Raise any due anticoagulant dose with the prescriber when bleeding is suspected.

Resuscitation, transfusion and possible return to theatre remain clinician-directed; use the authorised emergency blood-identification pathway, track perfusion/urine output and give timely blood-loss and laboratory-trend handover.

Falling platelets, abnormal clotting tests or a normal fibrinogen cannot independently determine DIC or blood-product selection; communicate clinical and laboratory trends while the team investigates.
Monitor temperature and ordered ionized calcium and potassium during major haemorrhage resuscitation; communicate abnormalities promptly and follow the authorised treatment pathway.
